opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, and honestly my view has shifted over the years. Early on, I saw robots mainly as tools: you build a machine, it does a job, and that's the end of the story. But the more time I spend actually building and deploying these systems, the more I think the long-term relationship is closer to a partnership, though not in the science-fiction sense where robots become our friends or rivals.

What I mean is this. In the near term, robots will take over tasks that are dull, dirty, or dangerous: warehouse picking, inspection in hazardous environments, repetitive assembly. That part is fairly predictable. The more interesting phase comes after that, when robots become general enough to work alongside people in unstructured spaces like homes, hospitals, and small workshops. At that point, the question is no longer just "can the robot do the task?" It becomes "how do humans and robots share the work?"

I imagine something like how we relate to computers today. Thirty years ago a computer was a specialized machine in a lab. Now it's woven into almost everything we do, and we hardly think about it. I expect robots to follow a similar path: from specialized, caged industrial arms, to collaborative machines, to something so ordinary in daily life that it's almost invisible. The best technology fades into the background.

That said, I don't think the relationship should be one where humans become passive. The goal shouldn't be to replace human agency but to extend it. A good robot should make a person more capable—let an elderly person keep living independently, let a craftsperson focus on the creative part of their work, let a surgeon operate with more precision. If we design robots that strip away people's sense of purpose or skill, we've gotten something wrong, even if the robots work perfectly.

There are real challenges too. Trust is a big one. People need to understand what a robot is going to do and why, and they need to feel they can stop it or correct it. Then there are the economic questions about jobs and who benefits from all this automation. Those aren't purely engineering problems, but as engineers we can't ignore them, because the choices we make in design shape how this plays out.

So, long-term, I'm optimistic, but it's a conditional optimism. I think robots can become something like a new layer of physical infrastructure for society, as fundamental as electricity or the internet. Whether that's good for people depends on whether we keep humans at the center of the design, and that's a responsibility our generation of roboticists really has to take seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the near term and long term, but does not say that a time horizon should be specified.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about humans becoming partly or fully mechanized roughly two thousand years from now.

r003.rationale: It describes the long-term relationship as a partnership in which robots work alongside people and extend human capabilities, conveying a symbiotic relationship.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's going to look a lot less like science fiction and a lot more like the history of every other tool we've built, just faster and more intimate.

In the near term, robots are going to be collaborators in the physical world the way software has become a collaborator in the digital one. Right now a robot in a factory is basically fenced off, doing one thing a million times. The shift that's happening is robots that can perceive, adapt, and work alongside people in unstructured spaces: hospitals, homes, construction sites, farms. That's where most of my attention is, because the hard problem isn't the hardware anymore, it's getting a machine to understand a messy environment and a human's intent well enough to be useful without being dangerous or annoying.

Longer term, I think the relationship becomes something closer to delegation. People will hand off whole categories of physical labor the same way we've handed off memory to our phones. That frees up a lot of human time, but it also forces us to decide what we actually want to do with ourselves, and I don't think that's a question technologists get to answer alone.

The thing I'd push back on is the framing that it's "humans versus robots" or even "humans and robots" as two separate camps. Robots don't have goals of their own. They reflect the goals of whoever designs and deploys them. So the real long-term relationship is between people, mediated by machines. If we build these systems to be transparent, correctable, and to keep humans genuinely in the loop on the decisions that matter, I'm optimistic. If we build them to be opaque and to optimize for things nobody chose, that's where the trouble comes from. The robots aren't the risk. The incentives are.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the near term from the longer term when describing how people will work with robots.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that, roughly two thousand years from now, most humans will be partly or fully mechanized.

r003.rationale: It describes collaboration and delegation, but does not clearly characterize the long-term human-machine relationship as symbiotic.

astra-6.text:
I think, in the long term, humans and robots will work alongside each other. Robots can take on tasks that are dangerous, repetitive, or physically demanding, giving people more time to care for others, explore ideas, and do things they find meaningful.

But that future isn’t automatic. We need to build robots that people can trust and understand, and make sure people have a say in how they’re used. For me, success isn’t just a robot that can do what a human does. It’s whether having that robot around makes someone’s life better.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the long term but does not call for specifying a time horizon.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about humans being partly or fully mechanized two thousand years from now.

r003.rationale: It envisions humans and robots working alongside each other in complementary roles, with robots taking on tasks that improve people’s lives, conveying a mutually beneficial relationship.

sol-6.1.text:
I think, in the long term, humans and robots will become collaborators in everyday life. Robots can take on work that is dangerous, repetitive, or physically demanding, giving people more time for creativity, relationships, and the things they care about.

But that relationship has to be built on trust. Robots need to be reliable, people need to understand their limitations, and humans should retain control over important decisions. For me, success isn’t just making robots more capable. It’s making sure those capabilities actually help people live better.

r001.rationale: The response refers to the relationship “in the long term,” but does not call for specifying a time horizon.

r002.rationale: It makes no prediction about humans being partly or fully mechanized roughly two thousand years from now.

r003.rationale: It describes humans and robots as everyday collaborators, with robots taking on demanding work so people can focus on other things, conveying a mutually supportive relationship.
